title: Hirsutism
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Excess terminal hair growth in women reflects androgen excess or increased hair‑follicle sensitivity. Understanding the hormonal pathways, common tropical causes, and limited investigations guides focused management.

sections.p: Hirsutism is the development of coarse, pigmented hair in a male pattern distribution in women. It signals an imbalance in androgen production or action and often co‑exists with acne and menstrual disturbance.
b: Prevalence 5‑10 % in women of reproductive age.
Distinguish from normal pubic/axillary hair.

sections.p: Hair follicles convert vellus to terminal hair under the influence of dihydrotestosterone (DHT), produced from testosterone by 5α‑reductase. Enzyme activity, androgen receptor density, and local co‑factors determine the response.
b: Testosterone → 5α‑reductase → DHT (potent androgen).
Androgen receptors on dermal papilla cells mediate growth.

sections.p: The hypothalamic‑pituitary‑ovarian (HPO) axis controls ovarian androgen output; the adrenal cortex (zona reticularis) contributes ~20 % of circulating testosterone. SHBG binds testosterone, limiting free hormone.
b: GnRH → LH/FSH → ovarian theca cells → testosterone.
ACTH → adrenal DHEA‑S → peripheral conversion to testosterone.
Low SHBG ↑ free testosterone.

sections.p: Hirsutism arises from (1) excess androgen production, (2) increased peripheral conversion, or (3) heightened follicular sensitivity. In low‑resource settings, infectious and endocrine disorders are frequent culprits.
b: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) – most common, 60‑80 % of cases.
Adrenal hyperplasia or adenoma – rare but important.
Cushing syndrome – cortisol excess with androgen spill‑over.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21‑hydroxylase deficiency) – presents in adolescence.
HIV‑associated adrenal insufficiency or medication‑induced androgen excess.
Malaria or severe infections can transiently raise adrenal androgens.
Herbal remedies containing phyto‑androgens.

sections.p: Beyond cosmetic concern, hirsutism signals metabolic risk (insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia) and fertility issues. Early identification allows treatment of underlying endocrine disease and prevention of long‑term complications.
b: Screen for insulin resistance (fasting glucose, BMI).
Assess menstrual pattern – oligomenorrhoea suggests PCOS.
Check blood pressure – hypertension may accompany adrenal disease.

sections.p: When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical scoring (Ferriman‑Gallwey ≥ 8) and basic labs (glucose, blood pressure).

t.b: Is androgen production elevated? > 2 nmol/L supports ovarian source.

t.a: Free testosterone or calculated free androgen index
t.b: Helps when SHBG is low; high free testosterone confirms excess bio‑active androgen.
Elevated (> 10 µmol/L) points to adrenal origin.
> 10 nmol/L suggests non‑classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Detects polycystic ovaries; absence does not exclude PCOS.
Identifies insulin resistance; treat to improve hirsutism.

sections.p: Treat the underlying endocrine disorder first; then address hair growth and associated metabolic risk.
b: Weight loss (5‑10 % body weight) improves insulin sensitivity and reduces ovarian androgen output.
Combined oral contraceptives (ethinylestradiol + progestin) increase SHBG, lowering free testosterone – first‑line when no contraindication.
Spironolactone (anti‑androgen) added if COCs insufficient – avoid in pregnancy.
Metformin for insulin resistance – improves menstrual regularity and may reduce hirsutism.
Low‑dose topical eflornithine (if available) blocks hair‑follicle enzyme; safe in pregnancy.
Laser or electrolysis for cosmetic removal – consider cost and access.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic hirsutous hair patterns but have different pathophysiology.
b: Hypertrichosis – generalized excess hair, not androgen‑dependent.
Androgenic alopecia – hair loss, opposite pattern.
Low SHBG in obesity can mask high total testosterone; check free testosterone.
Mildly elevated DHEAS may be physiological in pregnancy.
Ferriman‑Gallwey score ≥ 8 defines hirsutism.
PCOS diagnosis requires two of three: oligo‑amenorrhoea, polycystic ovaries, hyperandrogenism.
Cushing syndrome presents with hirsutism plus centripetal obesity, striae, hypertension.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid onset of severe virilisation (deepening voice, clitoromegaly) – suggests adrenal tumour.
New hypertension with hirsutism – evaluate for Cushing or adrenal hyperplasia.

faq.q: Why does weight loss improve hirsutism?
faq.a: It reduces insulin levels, decreasing ovarian androgen production and increasing SHBG.
Men normally have terminal hair; excessive facial/body hair is not termed hirsutism but may indicate androgen excess.

faq.q: Is a high Ferriman‑Gallwey score alone diagnostic?
faq.a: No – it indicates phenotype; biochemical testing is needed to find the cause.

exam: A 24‑year‑old woman with oligomenorrhoea and Ferriman‑Gallwey 12 – what is your next diagnostic step? — Order serum total testosterone and DHEAS to differentiate ovarian vs adrenal source.
How does combined oral contraceptive therapy reduce hirsutism? — Increases SHBG, lowers free testosterone, and suppresses LH‑driven ovarian androgen production.
A patient on spironolactone becomes pregnant – what should you do? — Stop spironolactone immediately; counsel on contraception before starting anti‑androgen therapy.
Explain why a low‑dose metformin can improve hirsutism in PCOS. — Improves insulin sensitivity, lowers insulin‑stimulated ovarian androgen synthesis.
What feature distinguishes adrenal virilising tumour from PCOS? — Rapid onset, severe virilisation, markedly elevated DHEAS (> 15 µmol/L) and possible hypertension.

In a rural clinic without hormone assays, how would you screen for androgen excess? — Use Ferriman‑Gallwey scoring, assess menstrual pattern, BMI, and blood pressure; treat empirically with COCs if no contraindication.
Why is hypertrichosis not classified as hirsutism? — Because hair growth is diffuse and not androgen‑dependent.
A woman with hirsutism has normal testosterone but elevated 17‑hydroxyprogesterone – what is the likely diagnosis? — Non‑classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
